title: Reading Practice 12 - Ocean Plastic Pollution
description: IELTS Academic Reading practice about the global crisis of plastic waste in oceans.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Ocean Plastic Pollution
stimuli.content:
A Plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental crises of the 21st century. Since the mass production of plastics began in the 1950s, humans have produced approximately 8.3 billion tonnes of plastic, of which only about 9% has been recycled. Much of the remainder has ended up in landfills or the natural environment, with an estimated 8 million tonnes entering the world's oceans every year. At current rates, scientists predict there will be more plastic than fish in the ocean by weight by 2050.

B The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, located between Hawaii and California, has become a symbol of ocean plastic pollution. Contrary to popular imagination, it is not a solid island of trash but rather a vast area of water containing elevated concentrations of microplastics, tiny fragments less than 5 millimetres in size. These microplastics are produced by the breakdown of larger plastic items through exposure to sunlight and wave action, and they are now found in virtually every marine environment on Earth.

C The impact of plastic pollution on marine life is devastating. Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, seabirds feed plastic fragments to their chicks, and whales have been found dead with stomachs full of plastic waste. Microplastics are ingested by organisms at every level of the marine food chain, from tiny zooplankton to large predators. Research has shown that microplastics can transfer toxic chemicals to organisms that ingest them and may also carry invasive species to new environments.

D Addressing ocean plastic pollution requires a combination of prevention, cleanup, and systemic change. Some countries have banned single-use plastics such as bags and straws, while others have implemented deposit-return schemes for bottles. Innovative cleanup technologies are being developed, though experts agree that preventing plastic from entering the ocean in the first place is far more effective than removing it afterwards.
